article-294.x: In regular employment, the employer may terminate an employee only for a just cause or when authorized by the Labor Code. An employee unjustly dismissed is entitled to reinstatement without loss of seniority rights and other privileges, and to full backwages, inclusive of allowances and other benefits, from the time compensation was withheld until actual reinstatement.
k: Security of tenure: dismissal only for just or authorized causes, and with due process.

Reliefs for illegal dismissal: reinstatement and full backwages. Separation pay may be given in lieu of reinstatement when reinstatement is no longer viable (strained relations, position abolished, and the like).
article-294.w: It implements the constitutional guarantee of security of tenure (Art. XIII, Sec. 3).
t: The employer bears the burden of proving a valid dismissal.
If the cause is valid but procedural due process was not observed, the dismissal stands and the employer pays nominal damages (Agabon).
q: What reliefs does an illegally dismissed employee get?

article-295.x: An employee is regular if engaged to perform activities usually necessary or desirable in the employer’s usual business or trade, whatever the written agreement or oral understanding says — unless the employment is for a specific project or undertaking whose completion was determined at engagement, or is seasonal and for the duration of the season. Any employee who has rendered at least one year of service, continuous or broken, becomes regular with respect to the activity for which he is employed.
k: Regular employment by nature of work (necessary or desirable).
Regular employment by length of service (casual employee with one year of service).
Exceptions: project employment and seasonal employment.
Fixed-term employment is valid if the term was knowingly and voluntarily agreed upon without force or improper pressure (Brent School).
article-295.w: It prevents employers from defeating security of tenure through labels in contracts.
t: The nature of the work, not the label in the contract, determines regular status.
Repeated rehiring of project employees for work necessary to the business may make them regular.
q: What are the two ways of becoming a regular employee?
When is a fixed-term contract valid?

d.h: Employment for a fixed period is not prohibited, even for work necessary or desirable to the business, if the term was knowingly and voluntarily agreed upon without force, duress or improper pressure. It is also valid if the parties dealt on more or less equal terms.
d.r: The leading case on fixed-term employment.

article-296.x: Probationary employment may not exceed six months from the start of work, unless covered by an apprenticeship agreement providing a longer period. A probationary employee may be terminated for a just cause, or for failing to qualify as a regular employee under reasonable standards made known to him at the time of engagement. One allowed to work after the probationary period is a regular employee.
k: Maximum six months (with recognized exceptions, e.g., apprenticeship; teachers under DepEd/CHED rules).
Standards for regularization must be made known at the time of engagement; otherwise the employee is deemed regular.
Termination: just cause or failure to meet the reasonable standards.
article-296.w: It gives the employer a fair chance to assess fitness, without allowing indefinite probation.
t: If the standards were not communicated at engagement, the employee is treated as regular from day one.
Working beyond the probationary period makes the employee regular.
q: What happens if regularization standards were not communicated at hiring?

article-297.x: An employer may terminate employment for just causes attributable to the employee: serious misconduct or wilful disobedience of lawful orders connected with work; gross and habitual neglect of duties; fraud or wilful breach of trust; commission of a crime against the employer, his family or representative; and analogous causes.
k: Five just causes.
Procedural due process: the two-notice rule (a notice specifying the grounds, an opportunity to be heard, then a notice of decision).
No separation pay is due for a just-cause dismissal, except as a measure of social justice in limited cases (not for serious misconduct or acts reflecting moral depravity).
article-297.w: Employers may protect their business from employee wrongdoing, but only through a fair process.
t: Loss of trust and confidence applies to employees occupying positions of trust, and must rest on clearly established facts.
If the cause is valid but notice was lacking, the dismissal is upheld, with nominal damages (Agabon).

d.h: When the dismissal is for a just cause but the employer did not comply with statutory due process, the dismissal is valid. The employer must pay nominal damages for violating the employee’s procedural rights.
d.r: The consequence of a procedural lapse in just-cause dismissals.

article-298.x: An employer may terminate employment because of the installation of labor-saving devices, redundancy, retrenchment to prevent losses, or the closing or cessation of operations. It must serve written notice on the workers and the DOLE at least one month before the intended date, and pay separation pay at the rates the article fixes.
k: Authorized causes: labor-saving devices and redundancy (separation pay of at least one month per year of service); retrenchment and closure not due to serious losses (one month or one-half month per year, whichever is higher).
Closure due to serious business losses: no separation pay is required.
One-month prior written notice to both the employee and the DOLE.
A fraction of at least six months is considered one whole year.
article-298.w: It recognizes management prerogative to respond to business realities, while cushioning workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own.
t: Retrenchment requires proof of actual or imminent substantial losses, usually through audited financial statements, and fair criteria in selecting who goes.
If notice is lacking for an authorized cause, the dismissal stands, with nominal damages (JAKA Food Processing).
q: Which authorized causes carry one month of pay per year of service?
What must be proved to justify retrenchment?

d.n: JAKA Food Processing Corp. v. Pacot
d.h: In a dismissal for an authorized cause without the required notices, the dismissal is valid but the employer pays nominal damages. The amount is higher than in just-cause cases, because the dismissal was initiated by the employer’s own exercise of management prerogative.

article-40.x: A non-resident foreign national may work in the Philippines only with an Alien Employment Permit (AEP) from DOLE. Both the foreign national seeking entry for work and the employer who wants to hire one must secure it. The permit issues only after DOLE finds that no Filipino is competent, able and willing to do the job at the time of application.
k: Who needs it: non-resident foreign nationals, and their domestic or foreign employers.
The core test: non-availability of a competent, able and willing Filipino (shown through the Labor Market Test).
For enterprises registered in preferred areas of investment, the permit may issue on the recommendation of the government agency charged with supervising the enterprise.
The AEP is separate from the visa: the Bureau of Immigration issues the work visa (e.g., the Sec. 9(g) pre-arranged employment visa) — both are needed.
t: Resident aliens are outside Art. 40; they register differently. The AEP rule applies to non-residents.
Since June 9, 2026, only the DOLE Central Office (Bureau of Local Employment) processes AEPs — not the Regional Offices.
Working without an AEP: the foreign national generally cannot obtain relief from the labor tribunals (WPP v. Galera; McBurnie v. Ganzon), unless the employer’s own fault caused the lapse (Rouche).
article-40.w: To reserve jobs for Filipinos when Filipinos can do them, while letting needed foreign skills in and transferring those skills to Filipino workers.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248, s. 2025 — Rules on the Employment of Foreign Nationals (in force February 2025)
i.s: Replaced D.O. 221-21. Before filing, the employer runs a Labor Market Test (publishing the vacancy) to show no competent, able and willing Filipino is available; DOLE also applies an Economic Needs Test. Certain employers must run an Understudy Training Program or Skills Development Program to transfer skills to at least two Filipino understudies. Exempt foreign nationals must secure a Certificate of Exemption.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248-A, s. 2025 — Supplemental Guidelines
i.s: Clarified D.O. 248: the training-program requirement applies only to certain employers (e.g., Foreign Investment Act registrants with fiscal incentives, public utilities, strategic or critical sectors); created technical working groups for training programs and the Economic Needs Test; listed exempt categories.

i.t: DOLE Administrative Order No. 199, s. 2026 and Department Order No. 248-B, s. 2026 — Centralization of AEP processing (effective June 9, 2026)
i.s: All new and renewal AEP applications, and every related function — receiving, evaluating, approving, issuing, renewing, cancelling, revoking and enforcing AEPs, Certificates of Exemption or Exclusion, training-program submissions, and the Economic Needs Test — moved from the Regional Offices to the DOLE Central Office, Bureau of Local Employment (BLE). Authority of Regional Directors passed to the BLE Director. Applications filed with Regional Offices up to June 8, 2026 were transferred to the BLE. Exception: motions for reconsideration of orders cancelling or revoking an AEP now go to the Director of the DOLE Legal Service.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248-C, s. 2026 — Simplified issuance (announced October 28, 2026)
i.s: Removes several documentary requirements (e.g., PCAB license, PRC special temporary permit, DOJ authority to employ alien, DENR authority) from the AEP filing, though compliance with those agencies’ laws remains required; cuts processing time from 15 to 10 working days, extendible once by 10; moves Labor Market Test notices from paid newspaper publication to the DOLE portal; lets employers file through their own HR staff. Takes effect 15 days after publication.

i.t: Centralized online filing and zero-contact policy (DOLE advisory, 2026)
i.s: AEP applications are filed through DOLE’s centralized online platform; transactions and inquiries follow a zero-contact policy.

d.h: The Labor Secretary validly cancelled the AEP of a foreign basketball coach. An employer’s right to choose its employees is limited by Art. 40, and the Secretary may consider whether the foreign national’s employment will serve the national interest. The comparison with a long-time resident foreign coach failed because Art. 40 covers only non-resident aliens.
d.r: The Secretary’s discretion under Art. 40, and the non-resident limit.

d.n: WPP Marketing Communications, Inc. v. Galera
d.h: A foreign national who worked without a valid work permit was found illegally dismissed but was denied employee benefits: one who comes to court with unclean hands cannot claim the protection of the Labor Code for an employment that violated it.
d.r: Effect of working without an AEP.

d.h: A foreign national’s labor complaint was dismissed because he did not show that he was qualified and authorized, through an employment permit, to work in the Philippines.

d.n: Rouche v. French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines
d.h: The foreign employee had held a valid AEP and 9(g) visa; the lapse came after his promotion and from the negligence of the employer’s counsel. Given those circumstances, WPP and McBurnie did not apply, and he was awarded relief for illegal dismissal.
d.r: An exception where the employer caused the lack of permit.

article-41.x: Once an AEP is issued, the foreign national may not transfer to another job or change employer without prior approval of the Secretary of Labor. A non-resident foreign national who entered as a tourist or on another non-working visa may not take up employment without first securing the permit.
t: A change of position or employer needs a new or amended AEP; working beyond the approved position is a violation.

i.t: DOLE Administrative Order No. 199, s. 2026 and Department Order No. 248-B, s. 2026 — Centralization of AEP processing (effective June 9, 2026)
i.s: All new and renewal AEP applications, and every related function — receiving, evaluating, approving, issuing, renewing, cancelling, revoking and enforcing AEPs, Certificates of Exemption or Exclusion, training-program submissions, and the Economic Needs Test — moved from the Regional Offices to the DOLE Central Office, Bureau of Local Employment (BLE). Authority of Regional Directors passed to the BLE Director. Applications filed with Regional Offices up to June 8, 2026 were transferred to the BLE. Exception: motions for reconsideration of orders cancelling or revoking an AEP now go to the Director of the DOLE Legal Service.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248-C, s. 2026 — Simplified issuance (announced October 28, 2026)
i.s: Removes several documentary requirements (e.g., PCAB license, PRC special temporary permit, DOJ authority to employ alien, DENR authority) from the AEP filing, though compliance with those agencies’ laws remains required; cuts processing time from 15 to 10 working days, extendible once by 10; moves Labor Market Test notices from paid newspaper publication to the DOLE portal; lets employers file through their own HR staff. Takes effect 15 days after publication.

article-42.x: Employers who already employed non-resident foreign nationals when the Code took effect had to submit a list of them to the Secretary of Labor; the Secretary may require the submission of training programs to replace them with Filipinos. Today the Understudy Training and Skills Development Programs under D.O. 248 carry this idea forward.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248, s. 2025 — Rules on the Employment of Foreign Nationals (in force February 2025)
i.s: Replaced D.O. 221-21. Before filing, the employer runs a Labor Market Test (publishing the vacancy) to show no competent, able and willing Filipino is available; DOLE also applies an Economic Needs Test. Certain employers must run an Understudy Training Program or Skills Development Program to transfer skills to at least two Filipino understudies. Exempt foreign nationals must secure a Certificate of Exemption.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 248-A, s. 2025 — Supplemental Guidelines
i.s: Clarified D.O. 248: the training-program requirement applies only to certain employers (e.g., Foreign Investment Act registrants with fiscal incentives, public utilities, strategic or critical sectors); created technical working groups for training programs and the Economic Needs Test; listed exempt categories.

article-82.x: Book III on hours of work, rest and leave applies to employees in all establishments, whether for profit or not, but not to government employees, managerial employees, field personnel, members of the employer’s family who depend on him for support, domestic helpers, persons in the personal service of another, and workers paid by results as determined by DOLE regulations.
t: Field personnel are non-agricultural employees who regularly work away from the principal place of business and whose actual hours of work cannot be determined with reasonable certainty.
Officers or members of a managerial staff are also excluded under the implementing rules.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I, Secs. 1–2
i.s: Coverage and exemptions.

article-83.x: The normal hours of work of any employee shall not exceed eight hours a day. Health personnel in cities and municipalities with a population of at least one million, or in hospitals and clinics with a bed capacity of at least one hundred, have a normal schedule of eight hours a day for five days a week.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I-A
i.s: Hours of work of hospital and clinic personnel.

article-84.x: Hours worked include all the time an employee is required to be on duty or at a prescribed workplace, and all time he is suffered or permitted to work. Rest periods of short duration during working hours are counted as hours worked.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I, Secs. 3–6
i.s: What counts as hours worked (waiting time, lectures, meetings, training).

article-85.x: The employer must give employees not less than sixty minutes time-off for their regular meals, subject to the regulations of the Secretary of Labor.
t: Shortened meal breaks of not less than twenty minutes are compensable hours worked under the implementing rules.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I, Sec. 7
i.s: Meal and rest periods, including shortened meal breaks.

article-86.x: Every employee is paid a night shift differential of not less than ten percent of his regular wage for each hour worked between ten o’clock in the evening and six o’clock in the morning.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule II
i.s: Night shift differential and how it combines with other premiums.

i.t: DOLE Handbook on Workers’ Statutory Monetary Benefits (latest edition)
i.s: DOLE’s guide to computing overtime, night shift, rest day, holiday and other premiums.

article-87.x: Work beyond eight hours a day may be performed if the employee is paid an additional compensation of at least twenty-five percent of the regular wage; work beyond eight hours on a holiday or rest day is paid an additional thirty percent of the rate for that day.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I, Secs. 8–9
i.s: Overtime pay and holiday or rest-day premiums.

i.t: DOLE Handbook on Workers’ Statutory Monetary Benefits (latest edition)
i.s: DOLE’s guide to computing overtime, night shift, rest day, holiday and other premiums.

article-88.x: Undertime work on any particular day shall not be offset by overtime work on any other day; permission to go on leave on a working day does not exempt the employer from paying overtime for work on another day.

article-89.x: Employees may be required to perform overtime work in cases of war or national emergency; urgent work to prevent loss of life or property or in case of imminent danger to public safety; urgent work on machines or equipment to avoid serious loss; work necessary to prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; and to complete work started before the eighth hour if necessary to prevent serious obstruction of the business.

i.t: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code (1989 compilation), Book III, Rule I, Sec. 10
i.s: When overtime may be compelled.

article-91.x: Every employer must give his employees a rest period of not less than twenty-four consecutive hours after every six consecutive normal work days. The employer schedules the rest day, but must respect the employee’s preference based on religious grounds.

article-93.x: Work on a scheduled rest day is paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent of the regular wage; work on a Sunday that is the employee’s rest day, or on a special holiday, likewise. Where the nature of the work requires work on Sunday and holidays without a regular rest day, the employee is paid an additional thirty percent for work on those days.

i.t: DOLE Handbook on Workers’ Statutory Monetary Benefits (latest edition)
i.s: DOLE’s guide to computing overtime, night shift, rest day, holiday and other premiums.

article-94.x: Every worker is paid his regular daily wage during regular holidays, except in retail and service establishments regularly employing less than ten workers. An employer who requires work on a regular holiday pays twice the regular rate.
t: Holiday pay is for regular holidays; special non-working days follow “no work, no pay” unless a company policy or CBA provides otherwise.

i.t: DOLE Handbook on Workers’ Statutory Monetary Benefits (latest edition)
i.s: DOLE’s guide to computing overtime, night shift, rest day, holiday and other premiums.

article-95.x: Every employee who has rendered at least one year of service is entitled to a yearly service incentive leave of five days with pay. It does not apply to those already enjoying at least five days of vacation leave with pay, or to establishments regularly employing less than ten employees, among others.
t: Unused service incentive leave is convertible to cash at the end of the year.

article-96.x: All service charges collected by hotels, restaurants and similar establishments are distributed completely and equally among the covered workers, except managerial employees (RA 11360, 2019). Service charges are not counted toward compliance with an increased minimum wage.
t: Before RA 11360, the split was 85% to employees and 15% to management.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 206, s. 2019
i.s: Implements RA 11360 on the full distribution of service charges.

article-97.x: Definitions for the wage provisions. “Wage” is the remuneration for work done, however fixed, and includes the fair and reasonable value of board, lodging or other facilities customarily furnished by the employer.
t: Facilities (for the employee’s benefit, deductible from wages) differ from supplements (for the employer’s benefit, not deductible).

article-99.x: Regional minimum wages are those prescribed by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards.

article-100.x: Nothing in Book III shall be construed to eliminate or in any way diminish supplements or other employee benefits being enjoyed at the time of the Code’s promulgation.
t: Non-diminution protects benefits that are given regularly and deliberately over a long period; it does not protect benefits given by error in interpreting a doubtful law.

d.n: Arco Metal Products Co. v. Samahan ng mga Manggagawa sa Arco Metal
d.h: An employer that for years paid benefits in full to employees who had not worked a full year could not later withdraw them, claiming error: the practice had ripened into a company practice protected by non-diminution.
d.r: When a benefit becomes a company practice.

article-102.x: Wages must be paid in legal tender; payment by promissory notes, vouchers, coupons, tokens or tickets is prohibited, even if requested by the employee. Payment by check or money order is allowed when customary or stipulated in a CBA, or in the cases the regulations allow.

article-103.x: Wages must be paid at least once every two weeks or twice a month at intervals not exceeding sixteen days. When payment cannot be made with that regularity because of force majeure, it must be made immediately after the cause ceases.

article-105.x: Wages are paid directly to the workers, except in case of force majeure (to a person authorized by the worker) or when the worker has died (to his heirs, without need of intestate proceedings).

article-106.x: An employer who contracts out work remains solidarily liable with the contractor for the employees’ wages. Labor-only contracting is prohibited: it exists when the contractor does not have substantial capital or investment in tools, equipment or machinery, and the workers perform activities directly related to the principal’s main business. The principal is then treated as the employer of the workers.
t: In legitimate contracting, the principal is still solidarily liable for unpaid wages and labor standards, as an indirect employer (Arts. 107 and 109).
k: Legitimate job contracting: an independent business with substantial capital, control over its workers, and a service distinct from the principal’s.
Labor-only contracting: the “contractor” merely supplies workers; principal and contractor are solidarily liable and the workers become the principal’s employees.

i.t: DOLE Department Order No. 174, s. 2017
i.s: Rules on contracting and subcontracting under Arts. 106–109: registration of contractors, substantial capital (₱5 million), and the badges of labor-only contracting. Replaced D.O. 18-A (2011).

article-107.x: An indirect employer is any person, partnership, association or corporation which, not being an employer, contracts with an independent contractor for the performance of any work, task, job or project. It is liable like a direct employer under Art. 106.

article-109.x: Every employer or indirect employer is responsible with his contractor or subcontractor for any violation of the Code; they are considered direct employers for purposes of civil liability.

article-110.x: In bankruptcy or liquidation of an employer’s business, workers enjoy first preference for unpaid wages and other monetary claims, ahead of other creditors, including the government.
t: The preference applies only in a formal bankruptcy or liquidation proceeding, and is a preference of credit, not a lien over specific property.

article-111.x: In cases of unlawful withholding of wages, the culpable party may be assessed attorney’s fees equivalent to ten percent of the amount of wages recovered.

article-113.x: No employer may make deductions from wages except when the worker is insured with his consent and the deduction pays the premium; for union dues where the right to check-off is recognized; and in cases authorized by law or by the Secretary of Labor.

article-116.x: It is unlawful for any person to withhold any amount from wages or to induce the worker to give up any part of his wages by force, stealth, intimidation, threat or any other means without the worker’s consent.

article-118.x: It is unlawful for an employer to refuse to pay or reduce wages and benefits, discharge or discriminate against an employee who has filed a complaint, instituted proceedings, or testified under Title II of Book III.

article-124.x: Standards for setting minimum wages: the needs of workers and their families, the employers’ capacity to pay, consumer price indices, the cost of living, wages in other sectors, and the requirements of economic and social development. Wage distortions resulting from a wage order are corrected through the grievance machinery or, if unresolved, voluntary arbitration in organized establishments, and the NCMB and then the NLRC in unorganized ones.
t: A wage distortion is a severe contraction of intentional quantitative differences in wage rates between employee groups; it cannot be a ground for a strike.

article-127.x: No wage order issued by a regional board may provide for wage rates lower than the statutory minimum wage rates prescribed by Congress.

article-128.x: Visitorial and enforcement power of the Secretary of Labor or his representatives: they may inspect workplaces and records, and issue compliance orders and writs of execution to enforce labor standards, notwithstanding Art. 129 and Art. 224 (formerly 217), where the employer-employee relationship still exists.
t: The power covers labor standards, regardless of the amount involved (RA 7730); the employer may contest it only on grounds that are documentary and verifiable from the records.

article-129.x: The DOLE regional director or a duly authorized hearing officer may hear and decide claims for wages and other monetary benefits arising from employer-employee relations, if the claimant does not seek reinstatement and the aggregate claim of each employee does not exceed five thousand pesos.

article-218.x: The State’s labor-relations policy: promote collective bargaining and voluntary modes of settling disputes (conciliation, mediation, arbitration), ensure workers’ participation in decision-making, and foster free and voluntary organization of a strong and united labor movement.

article-219.x: Definitions used in Book V, including employer, employee, labor organization, legitimate labor organization, company union, bargaining representative, unfair labor practice, labor dispute, strike, lockout and strike area.
t: A “labor dispute” exists regardless of whether the disputants stand in the proximate relation of employer and employee.

article-224.x: Labor Arbiters have original and exclusive jurisdiction over: unfair labor practice cases; termination disputes; cases accompanied by a claim for reinstatement involving wages, hours of work and other terms; claims for damages arising from employer-employee relations; cases arising from violations of Art. 279 (formerly 264) including legality of strikes and lockouts; and all other money claims arising from employer-employee relations exceeding five thousand pesos, except those of Kasambahay. The NLRC has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over their decisions.
t: The test is a reasonable causal connection between the claim and the employer-employee relationship; claims that need the application of civil law go to regular courts (San Miguel Corp. v. NLRC, 1988).
Disputes on interpretation of the CBA or company personnel policies go to the voluntary arbitrator (Art. 274).

article-229.x: Decisions of the Labor Arbiter are final and executory unless appealed to the NLRC within ten calendar days from receipt, on limited grounds. An employer’s appeal from a monetary award is perfected only upon posting of a cash or surety bond equal to the award. A decision ordering reinstatement is immediately executory even pending appeal: the employee is either admitted back to work or reinstated in the payroll, at the employer’s option.
t: Posting the bond is jurisdictional, though the Court allows a provisional bond of ten percent of the award while a motion to reduce is pending (McBurnie v. Ganzon, 2013).
Reinstatement pending appeal is self-executory; no writ of execution is needed.

article-233.x: Compromise agreements, including those resolving unfair labor practice cases, freely entered into and approved by DOLE’s mediators or conciliators, are final and binding, and the NLRC or any court will not assume jurisdiction over issues involved in them except in case of non-compliance or prima facie evidence that the settlement was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation or coercion.

article-240.x: Requirements for registration of a labor organization: the application, names and addresses of officers, the minutes of the organizational meetings, the names of all members comprising at least twenty percent of the employees in the bargaining unit, the annual financial reports if the applicant has been in existence for one or more years, and the constitution and by-laws.

article-247.x: Grounds for cancellation of union registration: misrepresentation, false statement or fraud in connection with the adoption or ratification of the constitution, by-laws and amendments, or the election of officers; and voluntary dissolution by the members.
t: RA 9481 (2007) narrowed the grounds; a union’s failure to file reports is no longer a ground for cancellation, and commingling of supervisory and rank-and-file employees is not a ground.

article-253.x: All persons employed in commercial, industrial and agricultural enterprises and in religious, charitable, medical or educational institutions, whether operating for profit or not, have the right to self-organization and to form, join or assist labor organizations for collective bargaining. Ambulant, intermittent and itinerant workers, the self-employed, rural workers and those without definite employers may form labor organizations for their mutual aid and protection.

article-255.x: Managerial employees are not eligible to join, assist or form any labor organization. Supervisory employees may not join the rank-and-file union but may form their own; the rank-and-file union and the supervisors’ union may affiliate with the same federation.
t: Confidential employees who assist managers in matters of labor relations are likewise excluded (doctrine of necessary implication).

article-258.x: Unfair labor practices violate the constitutional right of workers to self-organization, are inimical to the legitimate interests of labor and management, and disrupt industrial peace. They are both civil and criminal offenses; the civil aspect falls under the Labor Arbiters, and criminal prosecution needs a final judgment in the administrative case.

article-259.x: Unfair labor practices of employers: interfering with or coercing employees in the exercise of their right to self-organization; requiring as a condition of employment that a person not join a union; contracting out services to bust a union; initiating, dominating or assisting a labor organization (company union); discriminating to encourage or discourage union membership; dismissing or discriminating against an employee for testifying; violating the duty to bargain collectively; paying negotiation or attorney’s fees to the union or its officers as part of a settlement; and gross violation of the CBA.
t: ULP needs a connection to the employees’ right to self-organization. A mere CBA violation is ULP only if gross (flagrant or malicious refusal to comply with its economic provisions).

article-260.x: Unfair labor practices of labor organizations: restraining or coercing employees in their right to self-organization; causing the employer to discriminate against an employee; violating the duty to bargain collectively; causing or attempting to cause an employer to pay for services not performed (featherbedding); asking for or accepting negotiation fees from the employer; and gross violation of the CBA.

article-263.x: The duty to bargain collectively means the performance of a mutual obligation to meet and convene promptly and expeditiously in good faith to negotiate an agreement on wages, hours of work and all other terms and conditions of employment, but it does not compel any party to agree to a proposal or to make any concession.

article-265.x: Terms of a CBA: the representation aspect lasts five years; no petition questioning the majority status of the incumbent union may be entertained outside the sixty-day period immediately before the end of that five-year term (the freedom period). All other provisions are renegotiated not later than three years after execution.

article-267.x: The labor organization designated or selected by the majority of the employees in an appropriate bargaining unit is the exclusive representative of the employees in that unit for collective bargaining. Individual employees may still present grievances to the employer at any time.

article-268.x: In organized establishments, when a verified petition questioning the majority status of the incumbent bargaining agent is filed by a legitimate labor organization within the sixty-day freedom period, a certification election shall automatically be conducted, provided the petition is supported by the written consent of at least twenty-five percent of all the employees in the bargaining unit.

article-269.x: In unorganized establishments, a certification election is automatically conducted by the Med-Arbiter upon the filing of a petition by any legitimate labor organization, including a national union or federation that has issued a charter certificate to its local or chapter.
t: No minimum consent requirement applies in unorganized establishments.

article-271.x: In certification elections the employer is a bystander and has no right to oppose the petition or to take part in the proceedings, except to be notified or to ask for a certification election when asked to bargain.

article-273.x: Every CBA must provide a grievance machinery to settle grievances arising from the interpretation or implementation of the agreement and from the interpretation or enforcement of company personnel policies; unresolved grievances go to voluntary arbitration.

article-274.x: Voluntary arbitrators have original and exclusive jurisdiction over unresolved grievances arising from the interpretation or implementation of the CBA and from the interpretation or enforcement of company personnel policies. Gross violations of the CBA (flagrant refusal to comply with its economic provisions) are not treated as ULP and are resolved by them too.
t: Their decisions are appealed to the Court of Appeals by petition for review under Rule 43 (Luzon Development Bank v. Association of Luzon Development Bank Employees, 1995).

article-275.x: Voluntary arbitrators may, upon agreement of the parties, hear and decide all other labor disputes, including unfair labor practices and bargaining deadlocks.

article-278.x: Strikes, picketing and lockouts. A strike or lockout needs a notice to the NCMB: thirty days before the intended date in case of a bargaining deadlock, fifteen days in case of unfair labor practice (no notice period for union busting threatening the union’s existence). A strike vote by a majority of the bargaining unit, by secret ballot, must be reported to the NCMB at least seven days before the strike. In industries indispensable to the national interest, the Secretary of Labor may assume jurisdiction or certify the dispute to the NLRC, which automatically enjoins any strike or lockout and requires return to work.
t: A union officer who knowingly takes part in an illegal strike may be dismissed; an ordinary member is liable only for knowingly taking part in illegal acts during the strike.
Defiance of a return-to-work order makes the strike illegal and those who defy it lose their employment status.
k: Valid grounds: bargaining deadlock and unfair labor practice only.
Requirements: notice, cooling-off period, strike vote, report of the vote, and the seven-day waiting period after it.

article-279.x: Prohibited activities: no strike or lockout without first having bargained collectively, or after assumption of jurisdiction or certification, or during the pendency of cases submitted to voluntary arbitration; no obstruction of free ingress to or egress from the employer’s premises; no use of violence, coercion or intimidation; and no use of strikebreakers.

article-284.x: Foreigners may not engage in trade-union activities in the Philippines, except foreign nationals with valid working permits issued by DOLE (Alien Employment Permits) whose countries grant the same or similar rights to Filipino workers.
t: Read with Art. 40 (AEP) and the reciprocity condition.

article-299.x: An employer may terminate an employee found to be suffering from any disease whose continued employment is prohibited by law or prejudicial to his health or that of his co-employees, upon payment of separation pay of at least one month’s salary or one-half month’s salary for every year of service, whichever is greater, a fraction of at least six months counting as one whole year.
t: The implementing rules require a certification by a competent public health authority that the disease cannot be cured within six months even with proper medical treatment.

article-300.x: An employee may terminate the employment without just cause by serving written notice on the employer at least one month in advance; without notice, for serious insult, inhuman and unbearable treatment, commission of a crime by the employer against him or his family, and analogous causes.
t: Constructive dismissal: a resignation forced by the employer’s acts is treated as an illegal dismissal.

article-301.x: The bona fide suspension of the operation of a business or undertaking for a period not exceeding six months, or the fulfillment by the employee of a military or civic duty, does not terminate employment; the employer must reinstate the employee who indicates a desire to resume work not later than one month from the resumption of operations or relief from the duty.

article-302.x: Retirement: an employee may retire upon reaching the age fixed in a CBA or employment contract. Absent a retirement plan, an employee may retire at sixty (optional) and must retire at sixty-five (compulsory), if he has served at least five years, and is entitled to retirement pay of at least one-half month’s salary for every year of service, a fraction of at least six months counting as one year.
t: Underground mine workers may retire at fifty, and compulsorily at sixty, under RA 8558 (now RA 10757 also covers surface mine workers).
Retail, service and agricultural establishments employing not more than ten employees are exempt.
k: “One-half month salary” means 22.5 days: 15 days’ salary, plus one-twelfth of the 13th month pay, plus the cash equivalent of five days of service incentive leave.

article-306.x: All money claims arising from employer-employee relations accruing during the effectivity of the Code shall be filed within three years from the time the cause of action accrued; otherwise they are forever barred.
t: An action for illegal dismissal is an action for injury to rights and prescribes in four years (Art. 1146, Civil Code); the money claims attached to it prescribe in three years.
